Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff consumer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a debt collector's letter violates the FDCPA if the least sophisticated debtor could read it to have two or more meanings, one of which is inaccurate.

Cite at least six decisions of the Third Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### I. THE LETTER VIOLATES THE FDCPA BECAUSE THE LEAST SOPHISTICATED DEBTOR COULD READ IT TO HAVE TWO MEANINGS, ONE OF WHICH IS INACCURATE.

The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act prohibits a debt collector from using "any false, deceptive, or misleading representation or means in connection with the collection of any debt." 15 U.S.C. § 1692e. That prohibition reaches, among other things, "[t]he use of any false representation or deceptive means to collect or attempt to collect any debt." *Id.* § 1692e(10). Congress enacted the statute to protect "all consumers, the gullible as well as the shrewd." *Wilson v. Quadramed Corp.*, 225 F.3d 350, 354 (3d Cir. 2000) (citation omitted). To that end, this Court evaluates collection communications from the perspective of the "least sophisticated debtor." *Brown v. Card Serv. Ctr.*, 464 F.3d 450, 453 (3d Cir. 2006); *Rosenau v. Unifund Corp.*, 539 F.3d 218, 221 (3d Cir. 2008).

**A. The least sophisticated debtor standard.** The standard is "lower than simply examining whether particular language would deceive or mislead a reasonable debtor." *Brown*, 464 F.3d at 454 (citation omitted); *see also Campuzano-Burgos v. Midland Credit Mgmt., Inc.*, 550 F.3d 294, 298 (3d Cir. 2008). It presumes a debtor who may be naïve or unsophisticated, yet who reads the communication with some care and a basic level of understanding. *See Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354–55. Courts do not credit "bizarre or idiosyncratic interpretations." *Id.* at 354–55. But the standard exists to ensure that a collector's ambiguity is not resolved against the consumer the statute protects. *See Lesher v. Law Offices of Mitchell N. Kay, PC*, 650 F.3d 993, 997 (3d Cir. 2011).

**B. A letter that can reasonably be read two ways, one of them inaccurate, is deceptive.** Applying that standard, this Court has held that a collection letter is deceptive "when it can be reasonably read to have two or more different meanings, one of which is inaccurate." *Brown*, 464 F.3d at 455 (citation omitted); *accord Rosenau*, 539 F.3d at 221; *Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354. The inquiry therefore does not ask which reading the collector intended, or which a sophisticated reader would adopt. Where one reasonable reading is false or misleading, the statute is violated, however accurate the other reading may be. *See Caprio v. Healthcare Revenue Recovery Grp., LLC*, 709 F.3d 142, 148–51 (3d Cir. 2013) (holding collector's letter violated the Act where its language, read from the least sophisticated debtor's perspective, was open to a reading inconsistent with the debtor's statutory rights).

This rule rests on the statute's purpose. A collector controls the content of its letter and can eliminate ambiguity at no cost. A consumer, by contrast, may act on the inaccurate reading by paying a debt not owed in the amount demanded, forgoing a statutory right, or abandoning a dispute. Placing the risk of ambiguity on the collector is what the Act requires.

**C. The inaccurate reading is material.** A statement violates § 1692e only if it is materially false or misleading, meaning it could affect the least sophisticated debtor's ability to make an intelligent decision about the debt. *Jensen v. Pressler & Pressler*, 791 F.3d 413, 419–21 (3d Cir. 2015); *Douglass v. Convergent Outsourcing*, 765 F.3d 299, 303 (3d Cir. 2014). That requirement screens out technical errors that would not change a debtor's conduct. It does not excuse a letter whose inaccurate reading bears directly on what the debtor owes, to whom, or what the debtor may do in response.

**D. Application.** The Letter states that [quote operative language, with record cite]. One reasonable reading, and the one the collector presumably intended, is that [accurate meaning]. But the least sophisticated debtor could just as readily conclude that [inaccurate meaning]. That second reading is false because [explain inaccuracy, e.g., the amount, the creditor's identity, the consequences of nonpayment, or the debtor's § 1692g rights]. It is also not "bizarre or idiosyncratic." *Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354–55. It follows from the Letter's own words, structure, and placement of [relevant terms]. And it is material, because a debtor who adopted it could [pay an amount not owed, miss a dispute deadline, or forgo a right], which is precisely the harm § 1692e is meant to prevent. *See Jensen*, 791 F.3d at 419–21.

Because the Letter can reasonably be read in two ways, one of which is inaccurate and material, it is deceptive under § 1692e as a matter of law. *Brown*, 464 F.3d at 455; *Rosenau*, 539 F.3d at 221. Whether a letter is deceptive to the least sophisticated debtor is a question this Court may resolve as a matter of law where, as here, the Letter's text is undisputed. The judgment should be reversed.
